records.name_note: NC State's dedicated page for this hybrid renders an alphabetized Common Name(s) list, Hybrid Lavender then Lavandin, and its page-title parenthetical gives the same order; its Description prose opens with and uses the name Lavandin. RHS's dedicated page gives the common name lavandin (its page title reads Lavandula × intermedia | lavandin). Lavandin is used as the common name because NC State's Description prose and RHS's page lead with it. NC State calls the plant a hybrid cross between English Lavender and Portuguese Lavender, and RHS's Synonyms field lists Lavandula hybrida (angustifolia × latifolia) and Lavandula spica. Parent species pages were not used for any field.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Poison block for this hybrid is headed "Poisonous to Humans:" (human-scoped). Poison Severity: Low. Poison Symptoms: mild nausea and vomiting when consumed in large quantities. Poison Toxic Principle: Linalool, linalyl acetate. Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part: Flowers, Leaves, Stems. The page also states "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." No admissible source names cats or dogs for this hybrid, so no pet scoping is given. Edibility, from the same page: "The leaves, petals, and flowering tips can be eaten raw as a condiment, or in stews, soups, and salads. Its strong flavor prevents using it in large quantities. The flowers, both fresh and dried, can be used for making tea." The structured Edibility field reads: Leaves, petals, and flower tips. Leaves and flowers are therefore on both the edible list and the Poison Part list, while stems are on the Poison Part list only and are not named as edible; the edibility text and the symptom line set the same limit, large quantities.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: the NC State Poison block is human-scoped and no admissible source names cats or dogs for this hybrid; no genus-wide lavender pet listing was imported.

soil_drainage left null: NC State's structured Soil Drainage is Good Drainage plus Occasionally Dry, while its prose says dry to medium moist, well drained, alkaline soil and its Soil Texture list includes Clay, Loam (Silt) and Sand; that does not clearly earn fast, so it is not assigned. RHS gives only the bare Moisture value Well-drained.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH lists Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), both open-ended or band-based, and RHS lists pH as Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, so no floor or ceiling is supported.

water_regime and the day-interval fields left null: no admissible source frames watering for this plant; 'dry to medium moist' is a soil statement, and drought tolerance is a trait, not a watering instruction. NC State only says to provide good drainage to avoid root rot.

is_edible is true but conditional: NC State's Edibility text says the leaves, petals and flowering tips can be eaten raw as a condiment or in stews, soups and salads, that 'Its strong flavor prevents using it in large quantities', and that the flowers, fresh or dried, can be used for tea. Its human-scoped Poison block (Severity Low; Poison Part Flowers, Leaves, Stems) gives 'mild nausea and vomiting when consumed in large quantities.' Stems are on the Poison Part list and are not named as edible.

soil_base left null: no admissible source states a potting or bed mix; temperature, humidity, light footcandle and fertilizer fields have no admissible support and are left null. chill_damage_f left null: NC State gives no damage-onset temperature, only a winter-protection instruction ("If your location's winter temperatures dip to zero degrees, you will need to provide mulch or some other protective cover.") and the note that "Lavandin is somewhat less hardy than the parent plants"; its USDA Plant Hardiness Zone list (5a, 5b, 6a, 6b, 7a, 7b, 8a, 8b) and RHS's H5 rating are hardiness ratings, not onset figures.

RHS page for this hybrid lists size as Max Height 0.5-1 metres and Max Spread 0.5-1 metres (19.7-39.4 inches), and NC State's own Description prose says it grows larger than the parent plants ("maturing to a 2 to 4 foot mound", 24-48 inches); NC State's structured Dimensions block (Height and Width 2 ft. 0 in. - 3 ft. 0 in., 24-36 inches each) is used as the anchor.

Only NC State (plants.ces.ncsu.edu) and RHS were retrieved for this hybrid; MoBot's hybrid-level page could not be confirmed in this run (MoBot results found were cultivar or group pages, which support nothing).

is_houseplant is false: NC State's Plant Type field lists Herbaceous Perennial and Shrub, its USDA Plant Hardiness Zone field gives 5a-8b, and its Landscape Location field lists Coastal, Meadow, Patio, Pool/Hardscape, Recreational Play Area, Slope/Bank and Walkways; no admissible source frames the plant as a houseplant.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated Lavandula stoechas page gives its common names in the page-title parenthetical as an alphabetized list (Bract Lavender, Butterfly Lavender, French Lavender, Spanish Lavender, Topped Lavender), and its description leads with the name Spanish lavender; the page also lists the former name Stoechas officinarum. Sources split on the lead name: RHS's dedicated Lavandula stoechas page is titled 'Lavandula stoechas | French lavender' and lists Spanish lavender among its Other common names. RHS titles its Lavandula dentata page 'Lavandula dentata | French lavender' as well, so Spanish lavender, the name NC State's description leads with, is used here.
unknowns: RHS's dedicated Lavandula stoechas page (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/24039/lavandula-stoechas/details) is readable. Its Position field reads 'Full sun' and it carries the 'Plants for pollinators' badge, matching outdoor_sun_exposure and attracts_pollinators; its Moisture field reads only 'Well–drained', which neither adds to nor contradicts soil_drainage fast; its pH field reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral'; its hardiness rating is H4; it has no toxicity or edibility entry. Its size figures differ from NC State's: Max Height and Max Spread each read '0.5-1 metres' (about 20-39 in), and its description reads 'A bushy, upright evergreen shrub, to 60cm high and 40cm wide.' (about 24 in high and 16 in wide). NC State's species Dimensions block is kept as the size anchor. RHS leads with the name French lavender (see name_note). MoBot (plantfinder.mobot.org) refused connections and was not read.

is_edible left null: NC State's Edibility field says 'Not recommended for culinary use due to strong camphor flavor and piney scent.' That is a recommendation, not a statement that the plant is inedible or poisonous, and it does not say the plant is grown or used for food. The same page's separate Landscape Theme field does list 'Edible Garden' among its six values, and the page links the plant to a 'Pollinator and Culinary Garden' landscape, but neither says that any part is eaten; RHS's page does not address eating it. Nothing about culinary use was taken from L. angustifolia or L. × intermedia.
toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: the NC State page carries no toxicity or Problem-for-Cats/Dogs block, and none was inferred from the genus.

soil_drainage fast rests on the page prose (requires excellent soil drainage; gritty, sandy, or loamy, well-drained soil; poorly drained soils cause root rot), not on the bare Good Drainage tag. soil_base garden_bed rests on NC State's recommendation of the plant for mass plantings and mixed borders and its soil preference for gritty, sandy or loamy, well-drained soil; the page also places containers of it on a patio or in a small garden.

Hardiness: NC State states zones 8-9 (USDA Plant Hardiness Zone 8a, 8b, 9a, 9b, NC Region Coastal) and advises mulch or burlap against harsh cold winters. A zone rating is not a damage-onset temperature, so chill_damage_f is null.

Soil pH: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) bands together, and RHS's pH field reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral'. The acid and alkaline ends are open and RHS accepts both, so soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null.

water_regime null: the page gives no watering instruction, only 'Avoid overwatering' in the pest and problem paragraph, and drought tolerance, which is a trait and not a regime. Day-interval and dry-down fields are null for this in-ground shrub.

direct_sun_hours_max null: the page's 6-or-more-hours wording comes from the site-wide light-category label, not species prose. outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun only, from the Light field and the 'Prefers full sun' sentence.

is_houseplant false: no admissible source frames Spanish lavender as a houseplant or describes indoor culture. NC State presents it as a landscape plant for mass plantings, mixed borders and cottage, Mediterranean or pollinator gardens, and places its containers on a patio or in a small garden; its Landscape Location field lists Coastal, Container, Patio, Slope/Bank, Small Space and Walkways, with no Houseplants value. Temperature, humidity, light-fc, fertilizer and water-estimate fields are null because no admissible source gives them; NC State does warn that 'Inadequate sunlight and high nitrogen levels from fertilizer can cause poor flowering.'
Mature size 24-36 in is the species' own Dimensions block, not a cultivar figure; the page lists separate cultivar heights (for example 'Bandera Deep Rose' 6-9 in.) that were not used.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's dedicated Coreopsis grandiflora page tags the plant #non-toxic for cats, #non-toxic for horses and #non-toxic for dogs in its tag row. Those three tags are the page's only toxicity content: it carries no Poison block, no severity banner, no Problems field, no poison-part list and no handling warning. Its Plant Type field renders Herbaceous Perennial, Native Plant and Wildflower. RHS's dedicated page carries no Potentially harmful field. toxic_to_pets is false on the cat- and dog-scoped tags.
unknowns: MoBot Plant Finder (taxonid 277711, Coreopsis grandiflora) could not be fetched from this environment by curl/httpx (certificate errors), so no care field rests on it. Read in a browser at audit, its structured rows read 'Sun: Full sun' (excludes part_shade, which NC State's Light field and RHS's Position field both list, so part_shade was kept), 'Height: 1.50 to 2.50 feet' and 'Spread: 1.00 to 1.50 feet' (18-30 in and 12-18 in, narrower than NC State's 12-36 in anchor), and 'Common Name: large-flowered tickseed'; it states no toxicity.

Light: NC State's structured Light field lists only 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', while its description says the plant 'prefers a sunny location' and its tags include '#full sun tolerant'; RHS's Position field lists Full sun and Partial shade. Resolved to full_sun (NC State text + RHS) and part_shade (NC State field + RHS). direct_sun_hours_max left null because no species prose gives an hours figure (the 2-6 hours is the site-wide light-category legend).
Perennial reliability: NC State says it 'may not always be reliably perennial but will reseed itself in the garden'; it lists Life Cycle: Perennial and tag #self-seeding.

soil_drainage left null: NC State's Soil Drainage field is Good Drainage + Occasionally Dry and its text says 'well-drained soil in the drier portion of the garden' (sandy or rocky, adapts to clay if well-drained), while RHS's Moisture field is 'Moist but well-drained or Well-drained'. The sources lean differently, fast is not earned (no wet-tolerance statement either way is decisive), so no enum value was chosen.

soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State's pH field lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0); the Acid band is open-ended, and RHS lists acid, alkaline or neutral, so no closed ceiling or floor is supported.

water_regime and the day-interval/dry-down fields left null: NC State gives no watering instruction beyond tags '#drought tolerant #dry soils tolerant' (tolerance traits, not watering); RHS's cultivation sentence about keeping it moist in dry spells could not be confirmed as species-specific rather than genus text shared with sibling Coreopsis pages, and it is in-ground perennial anyway.

Size conflict: RHS lists Max Height and Max Spread of 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 inches), well below NC State's 1-3 ft (12-36 in) range and the NC State prose; NC State's dedicated-page figure was used as the anchor and the RHS figure is not reflected in the fields.

Toxicity: NC State's only toxicity evidence is three tags, '#non-toxic for cats', '#non-toxic for horses' and '#non-toxic for dogs'; no Poison block, symptom list or severity rating is present on the page. RHS's page carries no toxicity field, and MoBot's page (read in a browser at audit) states no toxicity.
is_edible left null: NC State names a landscape called 'Pollinator and Culinary Garden' but no source states that this plant is eaten or not edible.
Humidity, indoor temperature, fertilizing, chill damage and foot-candle fields have no admissible-source support (outdoor garden perennial) and are null.

Clemson HGIC's tickseed page is a multi-species spotlight, not a dedicated page for this taxon, so it was not cited. Cultivars 'Early Sunrise', 'SunKiss' and 'Sunray' were not used to supply any field.

common_name researched as 'Largeflower Tickseed', the third entry of NC State's alphabetized Common Name(s) list; landed as 'Large-flowered Tickseed', the name RHS's dedicated page leads with (the subtitle beneath its H1 and its page title). NC State's own Description spells it 'Large-Flower Tickseed', and MoBot's Common Name field (audit-reported, not fetchable here) reads 'large-flowered tickseed'. No landed common_name collides.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State Plant Toolbox (Iris sibirica page): the intro line says "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." and the 'Poisonous to Humans' block (human-scoped; this page carries no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag) lists Poison Severity: Low; Poison Symptoms: "Ingesting rhizome or root stock can cause stomach pain and vomiting. Contact with sap can cause skin irritation."; Poison Toxic Principle: Unidentified, possibly a glycoside; Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes; Poison Part: Roots, Sap/Juice. Handling warning (Insects, Diseases, and Other Plant Problems paragraph): "Wear gloves when handling this plant as the sap can cause skin irritation." Edibility field: "The rhizomes are not edible." Page tags include #contact dermatitis. NC State's Plant Type field renders Bulb, Herbaceous Perennial and Perennial; Bulb is not carried as a trait because the same page describes the plant as "Growing from rhizomes that will spread". RHS (Potentially harmful field): "Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." and "Pets: Harmful if eaten. For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants" - RHS does not name cats or dogs, so it is not used for toxic_to_pets. The sources differ on scope: NC State ties ingestion harm to the rhizome or root stock and skin irritation to the sap, while RHS's "Harmful if eaten." names no plant part.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: the only pet-related evidence is RHS's 'Pets: Harmful if eaten.', which names no animal (not cats or dogs); NC State's page has human-scoped poison data and no cat/dog tags.

is_houseplant is false: NC State's USDA Plant Hardiness Zone field gives 3a-8b and its Landscape Location field lists Coastal, Container, Meadow, Patio, Pond, Pool/Hardscape, Slope/Bank, Small Space and Walkways, with no Houseplants value; RHS rates it H7. No admissible source frames the plant as a houseplant.

NC State's Country Or Region Of Origin field reads 'Hybrid of two Asian species' and its Distribution field 'Central Europe,Russia, Japan, Korea', while its Description says the plant 'is native to Central and Eastern Europe'; its Plant Type field renders Bulb, Herbaceous Perennial and Perennial while the same page describes the plant as 'Growing from rhizomes that will spread'. Neither the origin field nor the Bulb value is carried into any field here.

water_regime left null: NC State says it is 'a moisture loving plant' and 'Until established, this plant prefers consistent moisture. It tolerates drought after it has been established' - a preference that is conditional on establishment, not a watering instruction; RHS Cultivation ('preferably moist but not waterlogged') is a soil statement. soil_drainage is therefore moderate (Good Drainage + Moist + Occasionally Wet; RHS 'Moist but well-drained'), not moisture_retentive and not fast.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0). The Acid band is open-ended, so it sets no floor, and the Neutral band's closed top (8.0) is not used as a ceiling because RHS's pH field reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral'. NC State's prose says it performs best in 'slightly acidic' soil but gives no number.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field lists Full sun and Partial Shade, mapped to full_sun and part_shade, and RHS's Position field lists Full sun and Partial shade. NC State's prose reads "Grow in full sun. Shade can have an effect on the plants performance. Too much shade may cause the plant to lay over and flowers to produce fewer blooms. In the southeast, protect from hot afternoon sun." The flop caution is about too much shade, not the partial-shade category both structured fields list, so part_shade is kept. The hour ranges inside NC State's Light values are its site-wide category legend, and no species-specific direct-sun hour figure exists, so direct_sun_hours_max is null.

Size sources differ: NC State Dimensions give Height 2 ft 0 in - 4 ft 0 in (24-48 in) and Width 2 ft 6 in - 3 ft 0 in (30-36 in), used here; NC State's Description adds 'Siberian Iris typically reaches a height of 2 feet, although some cultivars can be taller.'; RHS gives Max Height 1-1.5 metres and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (a narrow spread inconsistent with NC State), not used.

MoBot Plant Finder refuses this machine; searches at research and at audit surfaced only cultivar pages for Siberian iris (for example 'Butter and Sugar', 'White Swirl', 'Caesar's Brother', 'Sky Wings') and no dedicated Iris sibirica species page, so MoBot is not cited.
RHS hardiness rating H7; no onset chill figure, so chill_damage_f is null. No admissible fertilizing, humidity, temperature or light-intensity figures were captured.

common_name: both dedicated pages put Siberian Flag first (NC State's page-title parenthetical and alphabetized Common Name(s) list; RHS's page title and the subtitle beneath its H1), and the audit flagged the name for review. Siberian Iris is NC State's body-prose lead (its Description opens with it) and RHS's Other common names entry, and it is the name landed here; no landed common_name is Siberian Flag or Siberian Iris.

records.name_note: Admissible dedicated pages for this exact species split on the lead common name. NC State's page title reads "Salvia greggii (Autumn Sage, Red Chihuahuan Sage, Texas Sage)" and its Common Name(s) list (Autumn Sage, Red Chihuahuan Sage, Texas Sage) is alphabetized and in the same order as that title parenthetical; RHS's dedicated species profile has the page title "Salvia greggii | autumn sage"; UF/IFAS's dedicated page is headed "Salvia greggii Cherry Sage, Autumn Sage, Cherry Salvia" and lists "Common name(s): cherry sage, autumn sage, cherry salvia". Autumn Sage, the lead name on NC State and RHS, is used. NC State says S. greggii, S. microphylla and their hybrid Salvia × jamensis are difficult to distinguish from one another and that many modern cultivars are difficult to place in any of the three taxa, so only the dedicated S. greggii pages were used. NC State lists Texas Sage for this species, which it places in the mint family (Lamiaceae); its separate Leucophyllum frutescens page also uses Texas sage, for a desert shrub in the figwort family.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: the NC State and UF/IFAS pages for S. greggii carry no poison block, no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag and no toxicity statement, and RHS's species profile carries no Potentially harmful field; no toxicity is recorded or implied. is_edible is true per NC State's Edibility field (leaves used fresh or dried for seasonings and teas, flowers edible); UF/IFAS and RHS do not address eating, and no culinary-sage (S. officinalis) content was borrowed.

soil_drainage left null: NC State gives 'Good Drainage' plus 'Occasionally Dry' with texture 'High Organic Matter' and 'Shallow Rocky' (no explicit sharp/gritty requirement, so not fast; no moist/wet tag, so not clearly moderate); UF/IFAS says well-drained and cannot tolerate excessive moisture. Prose says it needs well-drained soil and tolerates rocky soil.
soil_ph_min/max left null: UF/IFAS lists soil tolerances 'acidic; alkaline; sand; loam; clay' with no numeric pH, and NC State gives no pH.
water_regime and related watering fields left null: sources give only drought tolerance and drainage traits, no watering statement.

Size sources disagree: NC State's species Dimensions give Height 2 ft. 0 in. - 3 ft. 0 in. and Width 2 ft. 0 in. - 3 ft. 0 in. (24-36 in, used as anchor) and its Description says it grows 2 to 3 feet tall and wide; UF/IFAS gives Height 1 to 2 feet and Spread 1 to 2 feet (12-24 in) in its Description fields but says in its Introduction that cherry sage generally attains a height of 6 to 18 inches; RHS's species profile gives Max Height and Max Spread 0.5-1 metres (about 19.7-39.4 in) and describes a bushy dwarf plant to 30-50cm tall.

Hardiness: NC State zones 6a-9b; UF/IFAS zones 7B through 11 and treated as annual in zone 7 and colder. Neither is a damage-onset temperature so chill_damage_f is null. NC State's 'Wild Thing' better-hardiness remark is a cultivar claim and was not used.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field lists Full sun and Partial Shade (2-6 hours); UF/IFAS's structured Light requirement reads 'plant grows in part shade/part sun' and its prose says 'Grow cherry sage in full sun to partial shade. Some shade is preferred in the warmest climates.' NC State's prose adds 'This sage prefers full sun but tolerates afternoon shade in regions with high summer heat.' part_sun not added because NC State's tag is Partial Shade.

is_houseplant is false: NC State's Plant Type field lists Herbaceous Perennial and Perennial and its USDA zones are 6a-9b, and it places the plant on slopes and banks, in naturalized areas and in borders, hedges and mass plantings; no admissible source frames it as a houseplant. Temperature, humidity, light_fc, fertilizer and direct_sun_hours_max have no admissible-source support and are null.

records.name_note: RHS's dedicated page gives white gaura as the profile name beneath its H1 and lists Lindheimer's beeblossom under Other common names. NC State's dedicated page's description opens with White Gaura; its Common Name(s) list is alphabetized, in the same order as the page-title parenthetical, and runs to eleven names, among them White Gaura, Whirling butterflies and Wand Flower. White Gaura is used because RHS leads with it and NC State's description opens with it. The species was moved from Gaura to Oenothera: NC State says so and its 'Previously known as' field lists Gaura filiformis var. munzii and Gaura lindheimeri, and RHS lists Gaura lindheimeri under Synonyms and notes 'This genus has changed from Gaura to Oenothera'. 'Whirling butterflies' appears in NC State's common-name list but is also a cultivar name ('Whirling Butterflies', white sterile blooms), so it cannot stand in for the species.
unknowns: NC State and RHS each have a dedicated Oenothera lindheimeri page that loads here; RHS gives the name status Correct. MoBot's dedicated page (kempercode c840) refuses scripted clients from this machine and was read in a browser at audit, so it is not cited and no field rests on it: there it leads with "Common Name: Lindheimer's beeblossom", its prose says "Gaura lindheimeri, commonly called gaura, is a herbaceous clump-forming perennial that is native to Texas and Louisiana.", and its rows read "Sun: Full sun" and "Spread: 1.00 to 2.00 feet". The pages differ on part shade, spread and pH, as the outdoor_sun_exposure, size and pH notes record. No dedicated page was found on the Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD or UGA domains, only multi-species lists.

No toxicity, pet-safety or edibility statement appears on the NC State page, and RHS's page carries no Potentially harmful field, so toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail and is_edible are null. Nothing was borrowed from other Oenothera (evening-primrose) species.

is_houseplant is false: NC State's Plant Type field lists Herbaceous Perennial and Wildflower and its USDA zones are 5a-9b; it places the plant along sunny borders, in containers, and in cottage gardens, wildflower meadows and naturalized areas, and never says houseplant or indoor. RHS is silent on indoor culture too.

soil_drainage is moderate from NC State's structured Soil Drainage field (Good Drainage, Moist) and its prose 'moist, well-drained soils'; the same page warns 'In poorly drained soils, root rot may occur.', which keeps it off the wet end, and RHS's Moisture field reads 'Moist but well–drained or Well–drained'. Soil pH is null: NC State's only pH value is the open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)' band and its prose adds acidic soils only, while RHS's pH field reads 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral'; no floor or ceiling is set.

soil_base is garden_bed: NC State recommends groups or mass plantings, sunny borders, cottage gardens, wildflower meadows and naturalized areas, and its soil prose names a sandy, loamy, acidic, moist, well-drained soil; it also allows a container planting.

water_regime is null: the page gives only soil adjectives (moist, well-drained) and the drought-tolerance trait, and no watering statement. The page does say 'The taproot helps make it drought and heat tolerant.' The page also says: 'Soil that is too rich will cause leaf growth and less flowering.' RHS's Cultivation, by contrast, reads 'Best grown in fertile, moist but well-drained soil in full sun; but dry soils and partial shade tolerated'. No fertilizer schedule or strength is given, so fertilizer fields are null.

direct_sun_hours_max is null: the only hour figures are the generic ones in NC State's light-category legend. Light fc, temperature and humidity fields have no admissible source figure. chill_damage_f is null because NC State's USDA zones 5a-9b are a hardiness range, not a damage-onset temperature.

Mature size comes from NC State's Dimensions block (Height 3 ft 0 in - 5 ft 0 in = 36-60 in; Width 1 ft 0 in - 2 ft 0 in = 12-24 in) for the species, not cultivars; NC State lists named cultivars with their own sizes (for example 'Dauphine' 5 to 7 feet tall, 'Corrie's Gold' 1.5 feet tall), which are excluded. RHS gives Max Height 1-1.5 metres (about 39-59 in) and Max Spread 0.5-1 metres (about 20-39 in); MoBot (audit-reported) gives Spread 1.00 to 2.00 feet.
'Wand Flower' appears in NC State's Common Name(s) list for this species; no dedicated page leads with it, so it was not used as the common name.

outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun only. NC State's Light field also lists 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', but its tag row carries '#partial shade tolerant' and its prose says 'It prefers full sun and will tolerate heat and humidity.'; RHS's Position field gives 'Full sun' only and its Cultivation reads 'Best grown in fertile, moist but well-drained soil in full sun; but dry soils and partial shade tolerated'; MoBot's Sun row (read in a browser at audit, not fetchable here) reads 'Sun: Full sun'. Partial shade appears in those sources as a tolerance, so part_shade is left out.

records.name_note: NC State and RHS both have dedicated pages for Salvia guaranitica and lead with different names. RHS leads with anise-scented sage, rendered beneath its H1, and that name is used here. NC State's page-title parenthetical lists (Anise Sage, Anise-scented Sage, Blue Anise Sage, Brazillian Sage); its Common Name(s) list is alphabetized and in the same order, so Anise-scented Sage is second there, after Anise Sage. NC State's own prose calls the plant 'Blue anise sage'.
unknowns: Two admissible dedicated pages were read: NC State (plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/salvia-guaranitica/) and RHS (www.rhs.org.uk/plants/16336/salvia-guaranitica/details). plantfinder.mobot.org refuses this client, hgic.clemson.edu returned 403 and edis.ifas.ufl.edu was not reachable. RHS agrees with NC State on sun (Position 'Full sun, Partial shade') and drainage (Moisture 'Moist but well–drained'). It gives pH only as 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', rates hardiness H3 and carries no toxicity section. It leads with the common name 'anise-scented sage'. Its size figures differ from NC State's: Max Height '1-1.5 metres' (about 39-59 in) and Max Spread '0.5-1 metres' (about 20-39 in), where NC State gives 2-5 ft (24-60 in) for both. NC State's species Dimensions block is kept as the size anchor.

Hardiness: NC State's prose says 'Although it is a tender perennial that is hardy in zones 8 to 10, it may be grown as an annual in cold-winter regions. 'Black and Blue' is hardier than other cultivars and will survive milder winters in zone 7 if well mulched.' The species range is zones 8-10; only the cultivar 'Black and Blue' is credited with zone 7 survival. NC State's structured USDA zone field reads 7b through 10b, which is wider than the species prose. There is no schema field for zones here and no damage-onset temperature is stated, so chill_damage_f is null.

Tuberous roots and spread: NC State says 'Blue anise sage produces tuberous roots that allow it to survive adverse conditions, but they also allow the plant to reproduce vegetatively. This plant gently spreads and fills a space. It can be readily contained in a large pot, but potted plants must be brought under protection when temperatures plummet.'

is_edible and toxicity: NC State has no Poison, Problem-for-Cats/Dogs or edibility content for this page. The anise-scented foliage implies nothing about eating; the only use noted is ethnobotanical (used by the Guarani Indians of Brazil as a sedative). is_edible, toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null. Nothing was taken from S. officinalis or from the hybrid 'Amistad'.

water_regime is null: 'evenly moist' appears only as a soil-preference adjective in the Description, with no watering statement; NC State's Resistance field lists Drought, and the prose says drought and heat tolerant once established. soil_drainage is moderate from the Good Drainage plus Moist pair, not moisture_retentive and not fast.
direct_sun_hours_max is null: the 6-or-more-hours and 2-6-hours figures are the site-wide light-category legend, not species prose. Partial Shade is mapped to part_shade.

is_houseplant is false: NC State's Plant Type field lists Herbaceous Perennial and Shrub and its USDA zones are 7b-10b; it frames the plant for borders, mass planting, containers and naturalized areas, and its pot advice ('It can be readily contained in a large pot, but potted plants must be brought under protection when temperatures plummet.') is outdoor container culture with winter protection, not houseplant culture. No admissible source frames it as a houseplant.
Not stated by NC State: humidity, temperature ranges, light in foot-candles, soil pH, fertilizer, and any watering interval, so those fields are null.

records.name_note: NC State carries this hybrid on two pages. The current-name page is titled Eriocapitella x hybrida and lists Anemone x hybrida under 'Previously known as:'; the older page is still titled Anemone x hybrida. RHS titles its page Anemone × hybrida and gives its Name Status as Correct, so the admissible sources split on the genus: NC State's current page uses Eriocapitella, while RHS and NC State's older page use Anemone. This record keeps the given name, which matches NC State's current page. Common names: the current NC State page lists Japanese Anemone and Windflower (alphabetized list, matching the page-title parenthetical), the older NC State page lists Japanese anemone, Thimbleflower and Windflower, and RHS's page title ends in Japanese anemone. The sources do not split on the primary common name. NC State writes the hybrid sign as ASCII x; it is normalised here to ×. Parent-species pages were not used.
records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox, current-name page (Eriocapitella x hybrida). The page carries the banner 'This plant has high severity poison characteristics.' and a 'Poisonous to Humans' block; that block is scoped to humans, and the page carries no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag. Poison Severity: High. Poison Symptoms text: 'TOXIC ONLY IF LARGE QUANTITIES EATEN. CAUSES SEVERE PAIN IN THE MOUTH IF EATEN! Poisonous through ingestion and dermatitis. (Poisonous parts: All parts when fresh).' followed by 'Symptoms may include: Inflammation and blistering upon contact with fresh sap; irritation of mouth, vomiting and diarrhea following ingestion.' The contact hazard sits inside that symptom text; the page gives no separate gloves or handling instruction. Poison Toxic Principle: Protoanemonin. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part, complete as rendered (seven values): Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems. Co-listed Problems tags: Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans. Plant Type values: Herbaceous Perennial, Perennial, Poisonous. The older NC State page (Anemone x hybrida) lists only Contact Dermatitis under Problems and has no Poison block. RHS and the other admissible sources give no toxicity information for this taxon. The current page's tag row also carries #poisonous.
unknowns: MoBot has no page for the hybrid itself (only cultivar pages such as 'Honorine Jobert' and 'September Charm', and a hupehensis parent page), so none were used. No admissible hybrid-specific page was found at Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD or UGA; none were used.
toxic_to_pets left null: NC State's Poison block is human-scoped, there is no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag, and no admissible source names cats or dogs.

Toxicity wording differs inside the NC State current page: the Poison Symptoms text says '(Poisonous parts: All parts when fresh)', while the separate Poison Part field renders seven values, Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems, with no freshness qualifier. Bark is listed although the same page's Plant Type field calls the plant an Herbaceous Perennial. The older NC State page lists only Contact Dermatitis under Problems and has no Poison block.

is_edible false rests on NC State's 'Poisonous through ingestion and dermatitis.' The same Poison Symptoms text opens 'TOXIC ONLY IF LARGE QUANTITIES EATEN. CAUSES SEVERE PAIN IN THE MOUTH IF EATEN!': NC State limits the toxic dose to large quantities but puts no quantity on the mouth-pain warning, and rates Poison Severity High. No admissible source describes any part as eaten.

water_regime left null: NC State says windflowers 'prefer moist but well-drained and fertile soils that are not allowed to dry out' (a soil preference, not a watering instruction) and cautions to avoid wet soils; RHS gives 'Moist but well-drained' as a moisture field and 'avoid excessive winter wet'. Neither is a watering statement. soil_drainage is moderate on that basis (NC State Good Drainage plus Moist, RHS Moist but well-drained).
soil_base garden_bed is an in-ground-planting reading from NC State's 'Found in: Landscape in flower gardens'; no source names a soil mix.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: RHS lists the pH field as Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, so no floor or ceiling is set; NC State gives no pH.

Size: the NC State figures come from the older Anemone x hybrida page only (the current-name page has no Dimensions block): height 2 ft 6 in to 3 ft 0 in (30-36 in) and width 4 ft 0 in to 6 ft 0 in (48-72 in). The older page's Description says 'They grow 1- 1.5 feet tall and up to 3 feet tall when in bloom.' RHS gives a larger Max Height 1-1.5 metres (39.4-59.1 in) and Max Spread 1.5-2.5 metres (59.1-98.4 in) over 2-5 years to maturity; NC State was used as the anchor.

Rhizomatous spread: the older NC State page says windflowers spread by rhizomes and make a good ground cover when given room to spread, and RHS describes suckering shoots and notes it can spread rapidly. No schema field holds this.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field (on both of its pages) lists 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' and 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', and RHS's Position field reads 'Full sun, Partial shade', so full_sun and part_shade both stand. The older NC State page adds a regional caution in its prose: 'In the south, they will do best in part shade to prevent burning the foliage and drying out.' That foliage-burn warning is scoped to the South and does not remove full sun from either structured field; in the South, NC State's stated best site is part shade.

NC State's partial-shade tag (2-6 hours) is a site-wide light-category legend, so direct_sun_hours_max is left null. Light foot-candles, temperature, humidity, fertilizer, chill damage, pH and watering intervals have no admissible-source figure for this taxon and are left null.

is_houseplant is false: NC State's current page lists Plant Type Herbaceous Perennial, Perennial and Poisonous, USDA zones 4a-8b and Landscape Location Woodland, and says the plant is 'Found in: Landscape in flower gardens'; no admissible source frames it as a houseplant.
NC State on the current page also carries 'wet soils intolerant' among its tags; this is a caution, not a drainage requirement. 'Honorine Jobert' and 'September Charm' cultivar pages were excluded.

The batch brief asked the researcher to drop 'Bark' from the Poison Part list (an herbaceous plant has none). The landed toxicity_detail keeps the list complete as NC State renders it, as the audit required and as the corpus does for other herbaceous plants (White False Indigo, Golden Club, Silver Ragwort, Angel Wings); the Bark/herbaceous mismatch is disclosed above rather than corrected.
